'''Stanisław Mieczysław Mazur''' ({{IPA|pol|ˈmazur|lang}}; 1 January 1905 – 5 November 1981) was a Polish [[mathematician]], a member of the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] and one of the leading representatives of the [[Lwów School of Mathematics]]

Mazur made important contributions to geometrical methods in linear and [[nonlinear functional analysis]] and to the study of [[Banach algebra]]s. He was also interested in [[summability theory]], [[infinite game]]s and [[computable function]]s.

==Life and career==
[[Image:MazurGes.jpg|thumb|right|Mazur awards a live goose to [[Per Enflo]], who solved Mazur's 1936 problem in the [[Scottish cafe|Scottish book]]. The photograph comes from the book ''Pół wieku matematyki polskiej 1920-1970'' ("Half a Century of Polish Mathematics 1920-1970").]]

Mazur was born on 1 January 1905 in [[Lwów]], then part of the [[Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria]] within [[Austria-Hungary]], to Tomasz Mazur and Aniela ({{nee|Zawrotniak}}).<ref name="ESLW">{{cite web|url=https://encyklopedia.slw.uw.edu.pl/articles/mazur-stanislaw-mieczyslaw/ |language=pl |title=MAZUR, Stanisław Mieczysław |author=Aleksandra Gomułczak, Anna Brożek, Jacek Jadacki, Roman Duda |work=Encyclodaedia of the Lwów-Warsaw School |publisher=Wydawnictwo Academicon |date=6 October 2025 |access-date=30 July 2026}}</ref> In 1923, he graduated from a [[gymnasium (school)|gymnasium]] in [[Lwów]]. Between 1923–1926, Mazur studied at the [[Jan Kazimierz University]] (now the [[University of Lviv]]).<ref name="MacTutor">{{cite web|url=https://mathshistory.st-andrews.ac.uk/Biographies/Mazur/ |title=Stanislaw Mieczyslaw Mazur |work=MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive |author=J.J. O'Connor, E. F. Robertson |access-date=30 July 2026}}</ref> In 1925, he completed an internship at the [[Sorbonne University|Sorbonne]] in [[Paris]].<ref name="ESLW"></ref> 

Mazur was a student of [[Stefan Banach]] at [[Jan Kazimierz University]]. His doctorate entitled ''O szeregach warunkowo sumowalnych'' (On Conditionally Summable Series), under Banach's supervision, was awarded in 1932.<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=13056}}</ref><ref name="ESLW"></ref> Mazur, with [[Juliusz Schauder]], was an Invited Speaker at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in 1936 in [[Oslo]].<ref>{{cite book|author=Mazur, S.|author2=Schauder, J.|chapter=Über ein Prinzip in der Variationsrechnung|title=Comptes rendus du Congrès international des mathématiciens: Oslo, 1936|volume=2|page=65|year=1937}}</ref> In 1936, he earned his habilitation and in 1947, he became a professor at the [[University of Łódź]] and the following year at the [[University of Warsaw]].<ref name="ESLW"></ref>

Mazur was a close collaborator with Banach at Lwów and was a member of the [[Lwów School of Mathematics]], where he participated in the mathematical activities at the [[Scottish Café]]. He was the author or co-author of 47 problems included in the [[Scottish Book]].<ref name="ESLW"></ref> On 6 November 1936, he posed the "[[Approximation problem|basis problem]]" of determining whether every [[Banach space]] has a [[Schauder basis]], with Mazur promising a "live goose" as a reward: 37 years later and in a ceremony that was broadcast throughout Poland, Mazur awarded a live goose to [[Per Enflo]] for constructing a counter-example.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.livescience.com/physics-mathematics/mathematics/a-79-year-old-mathematician-may-have-just-solved-an-infinite-dimension-puzzle-thats-vexed-theorists-for-decades |title=A 79-year-old mathematician may have just solved an infinite dimension puzzle that's vexed theorists for decades |website=livescience.com |author=Nathan Brownlowe |date=15 June 2023 |access-date=30 July 2026}}</ref>

In 1939, he became a deputy to the [[Elections to the People's Assemblies of Western Ukraine and Western Belorussia#People's Assemblies of Western Ukraine and Western Belorussia|People’s Assembly of Western Ukraine]]; from 1940 he served as a councillor on the Lviv City Council, and after the [[Soviet Union|Soviets]] returned in 1944 he joined the Main Board of the [[Union of Polish Patriots]].<ref>{{cite book | last = Duraczyński | first = Eugeniusz | title = Polska 1939–1945: dzieje polityczne |trans-title=Poland 1939–1945: A Political History | publisher = Książka i Wiedza | location = Warsaw | year = 1999 | isbn=}}</ref>

In 1946, Mazur was awarded the Officer's Cross of the [[Order of Polonia Restituta]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.dziennikustaw.gov.pl/mp/1946/s/25/42 |language=pl |title=Monitor Polski 1946 r. nr 25, poz. 42 |website=dziennikustaw.gov.pl |access-date=30 July 2026}}</ref> From 1948 Mazur worked at the [[University of Warsaw]]. He also worked at the [[Institute of Mathematics of the Polish Academy of Sciences|State Institute of Mathematics]], which was incorporated into the [[Polish Academy of Sciences]] in 1952.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.impan.pl/en/insitute/about-us/history |title=History |website=impan.pl |access-date=7 December 2024}}</ref> He was a foreign member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].<ref name="ESLW"></ref> In 1949, he received the [[Polish Mathematical Society#Stefan Banach Prize|Stefan Banach Prize]] conferred by the [[Polish Mathematical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ptm.org.pl/kategorie/konkursy/nagrody-glowne-ptm/nagroda-glowna-ptm-im-stefana-banacha|title=Laureates of Stefan Banach Prize|website=ptm.org.pl|access-date=2026-07-30}}</ref>

In 1978, he was awarded an honorary life membership in the Polish Mathematical Society and in 1980, an [[honorary doctorate]] at the University of Warsaw.<ref name="MacTutor"></ref> His notable doctoral students included [[Aleksander Pełczyński]] and [[Wiesław Żelazko]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.genealogy.math.ndsu.nodak.edu/id.php?id=13056&utm_source=copilot.com |title=Stanisław Mazur |work=Mathematics Genealogy Project |access-date=30 July 2026}}</ref>
